dt: {bc}being the two {bc}affecting or involving the one and the other

et: Middle English {it}bothe,{/it} a compound of {it}bo{/it} "two of a pair, both" and {it}the,{/it} definite article, going back to Old English {it}bā þā{/it} "both the, both these" (attested once late), from {it}bā,{/it} feminine and sometimes neuter nominative of {it}bēgen{/it} "both" + {it}þā,{/it} plural of {it}se, sēo, þæt,{/it} definite article; {it}bēgen, bā, bū{/it} (neuter) going back to Germanic {it}*bai{/it} (whence also Gothic {it}bai{/it} "both," neuter {it}ba{/it}), going back to Indo-European {it}*h{inf}2{/inf}(e)nt-b{sup}h{/sup}oh{inf}1{/inf}{/it} (with loss of the initial element and assimilation of the endings to the nominal declensions); other Germanic languages show early merger of the quantifier and the article, as Old Frisian {it}bēthe, beithe{/it} "both," Old Saxon {it}bēthie, bēthiu,{/it} Old High German {it}beide, bēde,{/it} Old Icelandic {it}báðir{/it} (but genitive {it}beggja,{/it} probably after {it}tveggja,{/it} genitive of {it}tveir{/it} "two") {ma}{mat|ambi-|}, {mat|the:1|}{/ma}

Middle English {it}bothe{/it} is also thought to reflect the Old Norse form exemplified by Old Icelandic {it}báðir,{/it} given the scarcity of the evidence for the collocation {it}bā þā{/it} in Old English, though other inflected forms of {it}begen, bā, bū{/it} followed by the inflected article are attested; see discussion and note on forms in {it}Oxford English Dictionary,{/it} third edition. The Old English masculine nominative {it}bēgen{/it} mirrors {it}twēgen,{/it} the masculine of "two" (compare {et_link|twain:3|twain:3}); the origin of the forms is uncertain—see discussion and bibliography in R. D. Fulk, {it}A Comparative Grammar of the Early Germanic Languages,{/it} John Benjamins, 2018, pp. 222-23.
